assembly_instructions: Presentation diorama, modelled at 0.6x of real metres (facts[] quote full-scale metres). Right-handed, +Y up. The single concrete ground plate spans X and Z; a raised brushed-steel divider strip along X at z=0 splits it into two halves. LEFT HALF (z>0) is the VISIBLE physical city: eight steel/concrete/glass towers, four of them set on concrete podiums and topped with rooftop mechanical units, two intersecting flat-box roads, a short bridge on two piers, and two streetlights. RIGHT HALF (z<0) is the INVISIBLE digital city rebuilt from infrastructure: eight 19-inch server racks at the mirror image (same X, negated Z) of the eight buildings so the urban footprint is preserved, each carrying two discrete brushed-steel server-blade units on its front face; a data-center spine running along X; three brushed-steel network-node towers carrying an overhead copper backbone; and eight copper data links, one per rack, dropping into the spine. Build order: lay the ground plate, set the divider strip, cast the four podiums and erect the eight buildings then their rooftop units, lay the roads, raise the bridge piers and deck, plant the streetlights; on the digital half erect the eight racks, mount the lower then upper blade unit on each, lay the data-center spine, raise the three network towers, string the overhead backbone, then run the eight copper data links. The connections graph is rooted at the ground plate. The layout is fully open — nothing is enclosed — and is intended to be viewed from a 3/4 angle.

info.japanese_name: 二都市ジオラマ（実体都市とデジタル都市）
info.english_name: Two-Cities Diorama (Physical City vs. Digital Twin)
info.summary: A split-plate diorama that places a small physical city beside its digital-infrastructure twin, where every building has a mirrored counterpart rebuilt from a populated server rack and a copper network. It visualises how the same urban footprint exists simultaneously as steel-and-concrete and as data.
info.description: The diorama sits on one 16 m x 11 m concrete ground plate divided by a centre strip; it is modelled at 0.6x so it stays within a compact viewing radius. The left half is a conventional skyline: eight buildings between 2.5 m and 6.0 m tall in concrete, welded steel and blue glass curtain wall, the four prominent towers set on concrete ground-floor podiums and crowned with rooftop mechanical units, served by two roads, a small bridge and streetlights. The right half is the 'invisible city' — the identical street footprint is mirrored across the divider, but each building is replaced by a dark-anodized 19-inch server rack (0.6 m wide, 1.0 m deep) of the same relative height, so a 6 m tower becomes a 6 m rack. Each rack carries two discrete brushed-steel server-blade units on its front face so the rack reads as populated. A 14 m data-center spine threads the racks together, three brushed-steel network-node towers carry an overhead copper backbone, and eight copper data links drop each rack into the spine. The piece is a teaching prop for a presentation slide, so it is deliberately open: no enclosures, no roofs, every component visible from a 3/4 camera.
